newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: PM says Slovaks favour NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: PM says Slovaks favour NATO membership.

text.p: Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar said on Thursday he believed a majority of Slovaks would vote for NATO membership in a referendum at the end of May.
"All current opinion polls show the majority of citizens will answer yes to the question of Slovakia's NATO membership," Meciar told Slovak television.
"The government is striving to ensure the biggest possible turnout to allow citizens to express their free will."
An opinion poll in December, conducted by the state-run Statistical Bureau, said 35.1 percent of the people supported NATO membership and 25.5 percent opposed it.

Slovakia, independent since Czechoslovakia split in two in 1993, has applied to be among the first new members of NATO, but its chances appear thin after Western criticism of the pace of its democratic reforms.
President Michal Kovac has set May 23 and 24 as the date of two referendums -- on NATO membership and on constitutional change to allow direct presidential elections.
He says Slovakia's hopes of being invited at NATO's Madrid summit in July to start membership negotiations were poor but a 'yes' vote in the referendum would help those who wanted to join.

The opposition claims the referendum questions -- on membership and on stationing nuclear warheads or foreign military units on Slovak territory -- are deliberately phrased to make people vote against membership and give political cover to Meciar's government.

Meciar, in the interview on Slovak television, said: "The first answer (membership) should be 'yes'. The answers to the second and third questions should lay the guidelines of the government position for the strategic talks."

He rejected Western doubts on Slovakia's path to democracy. "We are fulfilling all our commitments towards NATO and there is no objection (to Slovak performance) in the military sphere," he said. "In the development of democracy Slovakia is not lagging behind its neighbours."
Meciar, who has long sought to remove Kovac, a political rival, questioned whether the referendum on direct presidential elections would take place.
"There are constitutional obstacles to changes to the constitution by a referendum...and the government is preparing an appeal to the constitutional court to rule on this," he said.
The NATO referendum was approved by parliament, while that on presidential elections was the result of a petition organised by the opposition and supported by Kovac.
